content: Trachoma is recognized as the leading infectious cause of blindness globally. In 1996, the World Health Organization (WHO) initiated the Alliance for the Global Elimination of Trachoma by 2020, employing the 'SAFE' strategy, which includes surgery, antibiotics, facial cleanliness, and environmental improvement. This review focuses on the antibiotic component of the SAFE strategy, evaluating its effects on active trachoma, conjunctival infection with Chlamydia trachomatis, antibiotic resistance, and adverse effects. To gather evidence, relevant electronic databases and trial registries were searched, with the last search conducted on January 4, 2019. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were included if they met one of two criteria: (a) trials comparing topical or oral antibiotics to placebo or no treatment in individuals or communities with trachoma, or (b) trials comparing topical antibiotics to oral antibiotics in individuals or communities with trachoma. Studies examining different dosing strategies were also included. Standard Cochrane methods were used for data collection and analysis, and the GRADE approach was applied to assess the certainty of evidence. Antibiotics versus Control in Individuals Nine studies involving 1961 participants compared antibiotics to placebo or no treatment in individuals with active trachoma. These studies primarily enrolled children and young people. Antibiotics used included topical (oxy)tetracycline, doxycycline, and sulfonamides. The studies were generally poorly reported, making it difficult to assess the risk of bias. Low-certainty evidence suggested that antibiotics reduced active trachoma at three months (risk ratio [RR] 0.78, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.69 to 0.89) and 12 months (RR 0.74, 95% CI 0.55 to 1.00). For ocular infection, low-certainty evidence indicated a reduction at three months (RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.63 to 1.04) and 12 months (RR 0.25, 95% CI 0.08 to 0.78). None of these studies assessed antimicrobial resistance. No serious adverse effects were reported. Oral versus Topical Antibiotics in Individuals Eight studies involving 1583 participants compared oral antibiotics to topical antibiotics. Most participants were under 21 years of age. Oral antibiotics included azithromycin, sulfonamides, and doxycycline, while topical antibiotics included (oxy)tetracycline, azithromycin, and sulfonamides. These studies were also poorly reported, with low-certainty evidence suggesting little or no difference in the effect of oral versus topical antibiotics on active trachoma at three months (RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.16) and 12 months (RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.75 to 1.15). Evidence for ocular infection was very low-certainty. Antimicrobial resistance was not assessed. Adverse effects were minimal, with some reports of abdominal pain and nausea associated with azithromycin and a few cases of reactions to sulfonamides. Oral Azithromycin versus Control in Communities Four cluster-randomized studies compared oral azithromycin to no or delayed treatment in communities. Data on active trachoma at 12 months were available from two studies but could not be pooled due to differences in reporting. One high-quality study found a significant reduction in active trachoma prevalence 12 months after a single dose of azithromycin in high-prevalence communities (RR 0.58, 95% CI 0.52 to 0.65). A lower-quality study in low-prevalence communities reported similar infection rates between treated and untreated groups. Moderate-certainty evidence supported a reduction in active trachoma with treatment. Pooled data from two studies showed a reduction in ocular infection at 12 months (RR 0.36, 95% CI 0.31 to 0.43). High-certainty evidence indicated an increased risk of antibiotic resistance to Streptococcus pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus, and Escherichia coli in communities treated with azithromycin, with approximately five-fold risk ratios at 12 months. Resistance to penicillin or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole was not observed. No serious adverse events were reported, though azithromycin was associated with abdominal pain, vomiting, and nausea in about 10% of cases. Oral Azithromycin versus Topical Tetracycline in Communities Three cluster-randomized studies compared oral azithromycin to topical tetracycline. The evidence for active trachoma and ocular infection at three and 12 months was inconsistent and of low certainty. Due to significant heterogeneity, the data were not pooled. Antimicrobial resistance and adverse effects were not reported. Different Dosing Strategies Six studies examined different dosing strategies, including varying intervals for mass treatment, applying cessation rules, and strategies to increase treatment coverage. There was no strong evidence to support any variation in the recommended annual mass treatment. Conclusions Antibiotic treatment may reduce the risk of active trachoma and ocular infection in individuals infected with C. trachomatis compared to no treatment or placebo, though the magnitude of the effect is uncertain. Mass antibiotic treatment with a single dose of oral azithromycin reduces the prevalence of active trachoma and ocular infection in communities. There is no strong evidence to support changes to the recommended annual mass treatment schedule. However, there is evidence of an increased risk of antibiotic resistance in communities treated with antibiotics, particularly at 12 months.
